book_key: Vectors a and b are coinitial
our_answer: Vectors a and d are coinitial
note: Fig 10.6 was re-rendered from the source PDF at 10x and every arrowhead read individually. As printed: a lies along the TOP side with its arrowhead at the top-RIGHT corner (so a runs top-left -> top-right); b lies along the RIGHT side with its arrowhead at the bottom-right (top-right -> bottom-right); c lies along the BOTTOM side with its arrowhead at the bottom-LEFT (bottom-right -> bottom-left); d lies along the LEFT side with its arrowhead at the bottom-left (top-left -> bottom-left). Two arrowheads visibly converge at the bottom-left corner, which is c's head and d's head. Initial points are therefore a = top-left, b = top-right, c = bottom-right, d = top-left, so the coinitial pair is a and d, NOT a and b. The key's own remaining two entries corroborate our reading of the figure rather than its own (i): (ii) 'b and d are equal' requires b and d to BOTH run downwards, which is only true if b starts at the top-right, and (iii) 'a and c are collinear but not equal' requires a and c to be oppositely directed. The key entry (i) is the sole outlier and is a genuine answer-key error. RECOMMENDED BRACKET: [Textbook answer-key error: the official key gives "Vectors \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) are coinitial". In Fig 10.6 as printed, \(\vec{a}\) runs along the top side from the top-left corner to the top-right, \(\vec{b}\) runs down the right side from the top-right corner, \(\vec{c}\) runs along the bottom side from the bottom-right corner to the bottom-left, and \(\vec{d}\) runs down the left side from the top-left corner. So \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{d}\) share the initial point (the top-left corner), while \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) do not. The key's own remaining answers agree with this reading: (ii) requires \(\vec{b}\) and \(\vec{d}\) to both point downwards and (iii) requires \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{c}\) to be oppositely directed. The coinitial pair is \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{d}\).]
